readerTitle: Your task list says five weeks. Your history says eight.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (IT 서비스 회사, 식품 유통업체) + 실제 연구 (Buehler, Griffin & Ross 1994 계획 오류 연구, Kahneman & Lovallo 1993 내부 관점·외부 관점)
insight: 좋은 추정은 이번 일의 할 일 목록이 아니라, 비슷한 일이 실제로 얼마나 걸렸는지에서 출발해 차이만큼 조정하는 것이다.
misconception: 할 일을 빠짐없이 쪼개서 더하면 정확한 추정이 나온다. 모자라면 여유분을 조금 더하면 된다.

sources.text: Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381.
Kahneman, D., & Lovallo, D. (1993). Timid choices and bold forecasts: A cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science, 39(1), 17–31.
IT 서비스 회사와 식품 유통업체 사례, 차트의 주 단위 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Buehler 외(1994) 연구 1의 수치(졸업논문 완료 예상 평균 약 33.9일, 실제 약 55.5일, 최악의 경우 예상 약 48.6일, 예상일까지 끝낸 학생 약 30%)를 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 반올림해 "about 34", "about 55", "about 49", "fewer than a third"로 적었습니다.
내부 관점(inside view)과 외부 관점(outside view)이라는 이름이 Kahneman & Lovallo(1993)에서 소개되었는지 확인하세요.
가상 차트 수치: 과거 이전 작업 3건의 할 일 목록 추정 4·5·5주, 실제 7·8·10주. 모두 추정보다 길고, 이번 견적 문제의 과거 범위 7~10주와 일치합니다.
유통업체 문제: 할 일 목록 3개월, 첫 창고 실제 7개월, 공급업체가 본 다른 유통업체 사례 5~8개월. 정답 선택지의 5~8개월 범위와 약 6개월 계획은 이 수치와 맞습니다.

cards.title: Your task list says five weeks. Your history says eight.
body: An IT services firm is quoting a client's move to new email and file systems. A food distributor is planning its second depot. Both owners sit down and list every task. Both lists look complete.
Both estimates will be wrong in the same direction. The fix is somewhere most owners never look: their own past jobs.

image.label: Two desks: one with a long task list, one with a folder of past jobs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽 책상에는 체크리스트가 길게 늘어진 종이와 "5 weeks" 메모, 오른쪽 책상에는 지난 작업 폴더 더미와 "7–10 weeks" 메모. 두 메모 사이의 차이가 눈에 띄게. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you quote the client?
body: Your IT services firm is moving a 40-person office to new systems. Your team lists every task and adds them up: 5 weeks.
Your last three similar moves took 7, 8 and 10 weeks. The client wants a date in writing.

options.text: 5 weeks. This task list is the most detailed we've made.
options.feedback: You win the client with a sharp date, but you'll probably miss it. Past lists felt detailed too.

options.text: 6 weeks: the task list plus a 20% buffer
options.feedback: A buffer admits the list is short, which helps. But 6 weeks is still below every job you've actually done.

options.text: Start from 7–10 weeks, then adjust for what's different this time
options.feedback: You may sound slower than a rival. But your number rests on what really happened, not on what should happen.

cards.title: The task list vs the calendar
body: The IT firm pulled its last three office moves. Each time the plan looked thorough. Each time the job ran long.
Nobody was lazy. Task lists capture the work you can see. They miss the client who's slow to sign off, the sick week and the late delivery.
cards.callout: Every estimate was short. None by a little.

cards.title: Start from the outside view
body: Good **estimating** starts with a switch. The *inside view* builds a number from this job's own steps. The *outside view* asks how long jobs like this actually took, for you or for others.
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Dan Lovallo described these two views. Their advice: start outside, with real results from similar jobs. Then adjust for what makes this one different.

image.label: Two lenses: one zoomed into a task list, one zoomed out over many past jobs
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 돋보기 "Inside view"는 체크리스트 한 장을 크게 확대, 오른쪽 망원경 "Outside view"는 막대 여러 개(지난 작업들의 실제 기간)를 한눈에 보여줌. 오른쪽 막대들이 왼쪽 추정보다 길게.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams meet this every sprint. A feature "should" take three days. Check how long the last five similar features took from start to release, and the range is usually wider and later.

cards.title: Even worst cases come in too short.
body: In a 1994 study, psychologist Roger Buehler and colleagues asked students when they would finish their final-year thesis. On average they predicted about 34 days. They took about 55.
Fewer than a third finished by their own predicted date. Even their *worst-case* guesses, about 49 days, were too short.
Researchers call this the **planning fallacy**. We picture the job going to plan, even when we know past jobs didn't.

cards.title: Three steps to a better number
body: You don't need software or statistics. You need a short list of past jobs.
list: **Find similar jobs:** your own, or ask suppliers and peers what theirs took
**Use what actually happened:** the range, from the fastest to the slowest
**Adjust for real differences:** bigger, smaller, new team, known problem already solved
cards.callout: Give a range first. Commit to a point inside it only when you must.

cards.title: The comparison has to be fair.
body: The outside view is only as good as the jobs you compare against. A 10-person office move tells you little about a 200-person one.
With no history, borrow it. Suppliers, contractors and trade peers have seen dozens of similar jobs.
And a range can be hard to sell. Clients often want one date. Give one, but keep the range in your own plan and tell the client what would move it.

cards.title: Now it's a food distributor.
body: You're opening a second depot. Your list of steps (lease, racking, hiring drivers, new routes) adds up to 3 months.
Your first depot took 7 months. A racking supplier who has helped three other distributors says 5–8 months is normal. A big grocery client wants a start date.

image.label: Empty depot with racking half built and a calendar on the wall
image.brief: 반쯤 설치된 창고 선반, 바닥의 팔레트, 벽에 걸린 달력에 "3 months?"와 "5–8 months"가 함께 적혀 있음. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Promise 3 months and push the team hard
options.feedback: The client hears a fast date, but every real comparison says it's too short. A missed start can cost you the account.

options.text: Promise 7 months, exactly like the first depot
options.feedback: It's grounded in history, but one job is a thin sample. If last time's delays are already solved, you may be quoting too long.

options.text: Plan for about 6 months inside the 5–8 range, and tell the client what could move it
options.feedback: You give up a flashy date, but you earn trust. Your number rests on several real openings, adjusted for what you've learned.

cards.title: Ask how long it took, not how long it should take.
body: Start from what similar jobs actually took. Then adjust for what's truly different.
**Try it today:** pick a job you're estimating now. Write down three similar past jobs and how long each really took. Compare that range with your current plan.
